blocks.title: Timeline of discoveries (1915-1963)
rows: Macht and Mora coined the term 'psychopharmacology' while studying opioid alkaloids on rat behaviour in a circular maze
Sen & Bose (Indian physicians, Calcutta) reported antipsychotic properties of the plant Rauwolfia serpentina; reserpine was rediscovered by Kline in 1954

Cade (Australia) discovered the use of **lithium** compounds in mania, initially from a presumed relationship between urate metabolism and mania; **lithium** urate was prescribed to promote solubility of uric acid. He later noted the **lithium** ion itself had calming properties even in healthy controls

Presurgical antihistamine **chlorpromazine** shown to have antipsychotic effects independently by Delay and Deniker's team and by Charpentier (Rhone-Poulenc, France); in 1955 Delay coined the term neuroleptic

First true antidepressant: mood-lifting properties of iproniazid (an anti-tuberculosis treatment) led to the antidepressant class; hypertensive reactions precluded its large-scale use. **Imipramine**, manufactured as a **chlorpromazine** derivative, came to market soon after
First benzodiazepine, **chlordiazepoxide** (Librium), discovered serendipitously by Austrian scientist Leo Sternbach
Kuhn discovered that 'endogenous' depression responded best to **imipramine** (second tricyclic antidepressant **amitriptyline** introduced in 1961)

Janssen synthesised the butyrophenone **haloperidol** from pethidine; wide-scale antipsychotic use started. Antipsychotics came to be called major tranquilizers; barbiturates and benzodiazepines minor tranquilizers. Large-scale hospital discharges and deinstitutionalization started
Blackwell proposed the cheese reaction as the mechanism of monoamine oxidase inhibitor-associated hypertension

blocks.title: Timeline of discoveries (1970s-2005)
rows: **Fluoxetine** tested as a noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor but discarded for poor activity; later rediscovered as a serotonin reuptake inhibitor, reaching the market in 1987
Carlsson synthesised purpose-made selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor zimeldine, withdrawn because of hypersensitivity syndrome and demyelinating disease

Kane et al. rediscovered **clozapine** in a multicentre randomized design (**chlorpromazine** vs **clozapine**, 'treatment resistant' schizophrenia): ==4%== responded to **chlorpromazine**, ==30%== to **clozapine**
Reappraisal of suicides associated with antidepressant treatment: 'black box warning' for antidepressants in adolescents and children

Clinical Antipsychotic Trials of Intervention Effectiveness results published: reappraisal of atypical vs typical antipsychotics; the United Kingdom Cost Utility of the Latest Antipsychotic drugs in Schizophrenia Study study followed, showing no apparent economic gain from atypicals

blocks.subtopic: EXTERNAL UPDATE: Black box warning year
blocks.note: NEEDS VERIFICATION: The notes give no year for the 'black box warning' on antidepressants in adolescents and children (the '(period not given)' row of the 1970s-2005 timeline). Reviewer suggestion, not in the source: 2004.

blocks.text: Early psychopharmacology milestones: **lithium** (Cade 1949), **chlorpromazine** (Delay and Deniker / Charpentier 1950-52; term neuroleptic coined by Delay 1955), iproniazid as the first true antidepressant (1952), **chlordiazepoxide** (Sternbach 1954), **haloperidol** (Janssen 1958).

blocks.forTopic: Who discovered what: six name-drug pairs
blocks.mnemonic: Dogs Kiss Cats; Jackals Kill Bats

blocks.text: 'Major tranquilliser' = antipsychotic (**chlorpromazine**) - **NOT** **chlordiazepoxide** or secobarbital: the explanation says benzodiazepines and barbiturates were the **MINOR** tranquillisers. **Risperidone** and propofol are the other tempting options and are not the answer.

'**Clozapine**-Bowden' is the **INCORRECT** pair to spot. Kane et al. (1988) is the **clozapine** trial; Bowden led the first randomised study of **valproate** (**divalproex**) in acute mania (published 1994). The other four pairs - **Chlorpromazine**-Delay and Deniker, **Imipramine**-Kuhn, **Lithium**-John Cade, **Haloperidol**-Janssen - are correct.

Kane led the trial that proved **clozapine**'s effectiveness in resistant schizophrenia (Kane et al. 1988), which led to its strictly-limited reintroduction after it had been withdrawn for fatal agranulocytosis. Kretschmer, Cade, Kraepelin and Bleuler are distractors.

First antidepressant introduced = iproniazid, a monoamine oxidase inhibitor (chosen for its euphoric effects in tuberculosis patients) - **NOT** a tricyclic, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor, serotonin and noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor or tetracyclic. The explanation has tricyclic antidepressants arising later from **imipramine** and selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors later still, once serotonin was linked to depression.

Delay and Deniker = the tranquilising properties of **chlorpromazine** (Rhone-Poulenc, under Paul Charpentier); Cade, Kane and Bleuler are distractors. Spelling trap: the question writes 'Sen and Ghose' where the notes write 'Sen & Bose' (Rauwolfia, 1931).

items.text: **Q14**: psychotropic use of **lithium** = Cade (credited with reintroducing **lithium** to psychiatry for mania in 1949); the explanation adds that psychiatric use of **lithium** goes back to the mid-19th century.
**Q36**: reserpine is extracted from Rauwolfia serpentina (Indian snakeroot, Sarpagandha).
**Q3**: **clozapine** was withdrawn because of fatal agranulocytosis (not cost, efficacy, dosing or sedation) before Kane's landmark trial.
**Q37**: Bowden is the name tied to **valproate** in mania (first randomised **divalproex** study, 1994).

blocks.note: **Q3**: **clozapine** was withdrawn in the mid-1970s after several episodes of fatal agranulocytosis, before Kane's 1988 trial led to reintroduction with strict prescribing limits. The notes mention the Kane trial (==4%== vs ==30%== response) but not the withdrawal.

**Q37**: Bowden led the first randomised study of **valproate** (**divalproex**) in acute mania (published 1994), eight academic centres, with a **lithium** group; **divalproex** was significantly superior to placebo, and mixed-mania patients on **lithium** responded worse than on **divalproex**. Not in the notes.

Extra-pool question: Carlsson is associated with the dopamine hypothesis of schizophrenia. The explanation states that Arvid Carlsson made the seminal discovery in the late 1950s that dopamine is a transmitter in the mammalian brain. Not in the notes.

bullets.text: Psychopharmacology term coined 1915 (Macht and Mora, opioid alkaloids, rat circular maze).
Sen & Bose 1931 (Calcutta): antipsychotic properties of Rauwolfia serpentina; reserpine rediscovered by Kline 1954.
Cade 1949: lithium in mania (from a urate-metabolism hypothesis; lithium ion itself calming even in healthy controls).
Chlorpromazine antipsychotic effects shown 1950-52 by Delay and Deniker (and Charpentier); Delay coined 'neuroleptic' 1955.
Iproniazid (anti-TB) = first true antidepressant 1952; hypertensive reactions limited use; imipramine soon followed.
Chlordiazepoxide (Librium) discovered by Sternbach 1954; haloperidol synthesised by Janssen 1958 (from pethidine).
Kuhn 1958: 'endogenous' depression responded best to imipramine; amitriptyline (second tricyclic antidepressant) introduced 1961.
Antipsychotics were called major tranquillisers; barbiturates and benzodiazepines were called minor tranquillisers. Large-scale hospital discharges and deinstitutionalisation followed.
Blackwell 1963: the cheese reaction was proposed as the mechanism of monoamine oxidase inhibitor-associated hypertension.
Kane 1988 clozapine vs chlorpromazine in treatment-resistant schizophrenia: 30% vs 4% responded.
Zimeldine (purpose-made selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor, synthesised by Carlsson) withdrawn: hypersensitivity syndrome and demyelinating disease; fluoxetine marketed 1987.
Janssen synthesised risperidone 1989; 1990s 'Prozac era' of wide-scale antidepressant prescribing; later black box warning for antidepressants in children and adolescents.

Clinical Antipsychotic Trials of Intervention Effectiveness 2005 reappraised atypicals vs typicals; United Kingdom Cost Utility of the Latest Antipsychotic drugs in Schizophrenia Study showed no apparent economic gain from atypicals.
Pair trap: Clozapine-Kane (1988); Bowden = valproate in mania (1994) - 'Clozapine-Bowden' is the wrong pairing.
Carlsson: late-1950s discovery that dopamine is a transmitter in the mammalian brain (dopamine hypothesis of schizophrenia).

blocks.text: **Risperidone** is the benzisoxazole; **ziprasidone** is a benzisothiazole - the explanation itself says 'rather confusingly' - so the near-identical names are the trap. **Sulpiride** and **amisulpride** are substituted benzamides and **clozapine** is a dibenzodiazepine.

In 'choose the correct match', only droperidol: butyrophenone is right (**haloperidol**, droperidol and benperidol are the high-potency butyrophenones with troublesome extra-pyramidal side effects). The other four pairs (**risperidone**: dibenzoxapine (as worded in the question; reviewer: dibenzoxazepine, NEEDS VERIFICATION), **aripiprazole**: benzisothiazole, thioridazine: diphenyl butyl piperidine, **flupentixol**: dihydroindole) are wrong.

As printed in the notes, thioridazine appears under both piperidine derivatives and piperazine derivatives, and **ziprasidone** appears both as a benzisothiazole (antipsychotics list) and as a benzothiazolyl piperazine (other psychotropics list).

blocks.title: Antidepressants by chemical structure
rows: More potent; less sedating; more noradrenergic, less antihistaminic or anticholinergic than tertiary
Greater hepatotoxicity than **tranylcypromine**, a non hydrazine compound

blocks.text: The secondary amine is amoxapine; **clomipramine**, dothiepin, **amitriptyline** and **imipramine** are tertiary amines. Secondary amines (desipramine, amoxapine, **nortriptyline**, protriptyline) are more potent, less sedating, more noradrenergic and less antihistaminic/anticholinergic than tertiary.

**Buspirone**'s chemical structure = azaspirone-decanedione (azapirone/azaspirone), chemically distinct from other psychotropics; imidazopyridine, benzisoxazole, thienobenzodiazepine and aminoketone are the other (wrong) classes offered. It is a 5-**HT1A** partial agonist.
Z-drug classes are matched by name: **zopiclone** = cyclopyrrolone, **zolpidem** = imidazopyridine, zaleplon = pyrazolopyrimidine. Butyrophenone and azaspirones are the distractor classes offered.

blocks.note: NEEDS VERIFICATION: Sibutramine is listed among the serotonin and noradrenaline reuptake inhibitors in the notes, but it was an anti-obesity drug, not an antidepressant, and was withdrawn in 2010 because of cardiovascular risk.

NEEDS VERIFICATION: The notes give only the label 'noradrenaline dopamine disinhibitor'. Its receptor action is melatonin MT1/MT2 receptor agonism plus serotonin 5-HT2C receptor antagonism; 5-HT2C antagonism disinhibits noradrenaline and dopamine release in the frontal cortex. Exam questions often test the receptor action.

blocks.text: Serotonin and noradrenaline reuptake inhibitors per the explanation: **duloxetine**, **venlafaxine**, desvenlafaxine, milnacipran and levomilnacipran. The notes' serotonin and noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor list (**venlafaxine**, milnacipran, **duloxetine**, sibutramine) differs - the question adds desvenlafaxine and levomilnacipran. **Reboxetine**, **bupropion**, **galantamine** and **aripiprazole** are the distractors.

blocks.forTopic: Serotonin and noradrenaline reuptake inhibitors (Q22 explanation)
blocks.mnemonic: DVD ML - "Dull Vets Dream Mostly Lazily"

blocks.text: Term trap: the question calls **bupropion** a norepinephrine and dopamine re-uptake inhibitor, whereas the notes label it dopamine reuptake inhibitor - both are stated. It is indicated for depression but licensed in the United Kingdom only for nicotine dependence.

**Risperidone** - **paliperidone** is the correct drug-metabolite pair (**paliperidone** is the major active metabolite of **risperidone**). **Citalopram** - **escitalopram** is **NOT** a metabolite pair: **escitalopram** is the pure S enantiomer. **Naloxone**-**naltrexone**, **imipramine**-nomifensine and **fluoxetine**-**duloxetine** are also wrong.

Xanomeline (acts via muscarinic M1/M4 receptor agonism) underwent phase 3 trials in schizophrenia: trend toward improved cognition in Alzheimer's and robust dose-dependent reductions in psychotic symptoms in Alzheimer's disease; in schizophrenia early trials showed efficacy in positive and negative symptoms plus improved verbal learning and short-term memory, but with a high degree of gastrointestinal side effects.

blocks.note: NEEDS VERIFICATION: Xanomeline combined with trospium (a peripherally acting muscarinic antagonist that reduces the gastrointestinal and other peripheral cholinergic side effects) was approved by the United States Food and Drug Administration in September 2024 for schizophrenia in adults (brand name Cobenfy). The notes describe xanomeline only as 'in phase 3'; older exam questions may still use that wording.

blocks.text: **Ketamine**, a glutamate N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor antagonist, has shown rapid antidepressant effects in treatment-resistant depression; large-scale trials were under way.

blocks.note: NEEDS VERIFICATION: Esketamine nasal spray (the S-enantiomer of ketamine) was approved in the United States in 2019 for treatment-resistant depression alongside an oral antidepressant, and is licensed in Europe; the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence did not recommend it for routine National Health Service use. The notes say only that large-scale ketamine trials are under way.

blocks.text: Pomaglumetad methionil (**LY2140023**), a metabotropic glutamate receptor 2/3 agonist, looked promising in phase 2 as add-on therapy for positive and negative symptoms of schizophrenia, but the result was not replicated in a later study, mostly due to high placebo response. It has no affinity for dopamine receptors.

blocks.note: NEEDS VERIFICATION: Eli Lilly stopped development of pomaglumetad methionil for schizophrenia in 2012 after failed phase 3 results.

items.text: **Q2**: **olanzapine** is the thienobenzodiazepine (multi-receptor antagonism; structurally related to **clozapine**).
**Q46**: **haloperidol** is the butyrophenone (not **chlorpromazine**, thioridazine, flupenthixol or **zuclopenthixol**).
**Q50**: **flupentixol** (and **zuclopenthixol**) are thioxanthenes with moderate sedative, antimuscarinic and extra-pyramidal effects.
**Q45**: **escitalopram** is the enantiomer of another antidepressant (pure S enantiomer of **citalopram**) - not a metabolite of it.

**Q53**: **moclobemide** is the reversible monoamine oxidase inhibitor (reversible inhibitor of monoamine oxidase A); the 'cheese reaction' is less likely with reversible inhibitor of monoamine oxidase As than with traditional monoamine oxidase inhibitors.
**Q29**: **duloxetine** and milnacipran are serotonin and noradrenaline reuptake inhibitors (serotonergic and noradrenergic reuptake inhibitors).

blocks.note: **Q55**: **paliperidone** is a benzisoxazole derivative and the major active metabolite of **risperidone**. The notes list only **risperidone** under benzisoxazole; **paliperidone** is not named.

**Q7**: **alprazolam** is a benzodiazepine (benzodiazepines share an effect on benzodiazepine receptors, which modulate gamma-aminobutyric acid activity; onset is quickest for **diazepam**, **lorazepam**, **alprazolam**, triazolam, estazolam). Notes do not list benzodiazepines by structure.
**Q17**: **buspirone** is a 5-**HT1A** partial agonist. The notes give only its chemical class.
**Q28**: **bupropion** (aminoketone) has a dose-related seizure risk (particularly instant-release; lower with slow-release under 300 mg/day) and should be avoided in epilepsy. Not in the notes.
**Q33**: **rivastigmine** is a reversible non-competitive inhibitor of acetylcholinesterase (also inhibits butyrylcholinesterase). Not in the notes.
**Q51**: **memantine** is an N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor antagonist. Not in the notes.
**Q39**: lofexidine is an alpha-2 adrenergic agonist, useful for opioid withdrawal symptoms. Not in the notes.
**Q41**: **acamprosate** is a synthetic taurine analogue, a functional glutamatergic N-methyl-D-aspartate antagonist that also increases gamma-aminobutyric acid-ergic function. Not in the notes.
**Q4**: cyproterone acetate is an anti-androgen (testosterone antagonist) with evidence in hypersexuality and paraphilias. Not in the notes.

**Q5**: selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors are first-line for obsessive-compulsive disorder (no clear superiority of one agent, high doses usually needed, at least 12 weeks for response, long-term therapy). Not in the notes.
**Q21**: sodium **valproate** is the answer; National Institute for Health and Care Excellence recommends mixed affective episodes be treated as manic episodes. Not in the notes.

blocks.text: Mixed affective episode, bank answer = sodium **valproate** (**carbamazepine**, **gabapentin**, **clonazepam** and **lamotrigine** are the other options). National Institute for Health and Care Excellence recommends mixed episodes be treated as manic episodes; antipsychotics, **lithium** and **valproate** are first-line, and **lamotrigine** is **NOT** offered for mania. The extra-pool version of this question keys **olanzapine** instead (see gap below).

blocks.note: Extra-pool question: **olanzapine** is the antipsychotic keyed for mixed affective states in bipolar disorder. The explanation cites a Cochrane review and British Association of Psychopharmacology guidelines: **olanzapine** may prevent further mood episodes in patients who responded to it during an index manic or mixed episode and who did not previously respond satisfactorily to **lithium** or **valproate**. Not in the notes.
**Q40**: thyroid hormone is used in depression (tri-iodothyronine as second-line augmentation in treatment-resistant depression). Not in the notes.

**Q56**: a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor or **venlafaxine** plus **mianserin** or **mirtazapine** has literature support and National Institute for Health and Care Excellence recommendation (theoretical serotonin-syndrome risk; blood dyscrasia with **mianserin**). Not in the notes.

**Q44**: drugs acting on intracellular secretase enzymes (beta-site amyloid precursor protein cleaving enzyme 1, needed to generate amyloid-beta) are a potential advance in dementia treatment. Not in the notes.
**Q43**: no recommendation exists for drug prevention of dementia in mild cognitive impairment. Not in the notes.

bullets.text: Antipsychotic chemical classes: butyrophenones (haloperidol, droperidol), thioxanthenes (flupenthixol, zuclopenthixol), benzamides (amisulpride, sulpiride), olanzapine thienobenzodiazepine, clozapine dibenzodiazepine, quetiapine dibenzothiazepine, risperidone benzisoxazole.

Phenothiazines: aliphatic (chlorpromazine, promazine, triflupromazine), piperidine (thioridazine), piperazine (trifluoperazine, fluphenazine, perphenazine). Thioridazine is printed under both piperidine and piperazine in the notes.

Loxapine = dibenzoxapine; molindone = dihydroindoles (class names as printed in the notes; Question 8 pairs these class names wrongly with risperidone and flupentixol). Reviewer correction (not in the source), NEEDS VERIFICATION: dibenzoxazepine and dihydroindolone.
Pimozide is the diphenylbutylpiperidine (long half-life); aripiprazole is an arylpiperidylindole (quinolone; reviewer: quinolinone, NEEDS VERIFICATION); ziprasidone a benzisothiazole.

Tertiary amine tricyclic antidepressants (imipramine, amitriptyline, clomipramine, dosulepin, trimipramine) vs secondary amines (desipramine, amoxapine, nortriptyline, protriptyline): secondary more potent, less sedating, more noradrenergic, less antihistaminic/anticholinergic.
Hydrazine monoamine oxidase inhibitors: phenelzine, isocarboxazid (greater hepatotoxicity than non-hydrazine tranylcypromine); bupropion aminoketone (amphetamine-like).
Other psychotropics by class: buspirone azaspirodecanedione; zolpidem imidazopyridine; zaleplon pyrazolopyrimidine; zopiclone cyclopyrrolone; trazodone/nefazodone triazolopyridines.

By mechanism: selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs), serotonin and noradrenaline reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs: venlafaxine, milnacipran, duloxetine, sibutramine), noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor (NARI) reboxetine, noradrenaline dopamine disinhibitor (NDDI) agomelatine, noradrenergic and specific serotonergic antagonist (NaSSA) mirtazapine/mianserin, dopamine reuptake inhibitor (DARI) bupropion, reversible inhibitor of monoamine oxidase A (RIMA) moclobemide, serotonin antagonist and reuptake inhibitor (SARI) nefazodone/trazodone.
Escitalopram is the S enantiomer of citalopram.

Novel agents: xanomeline (muscarinic M1/M4 receptor agonist; GI side effects), ketamine (N-methyl-D-aspartate antagonist; rapid antidepressant effect), pomaglumetad (mGluR2/3 agonist; not replicated, high placebo response).
Risperidone = benzisoxazole; ziprasidone = benzisothiazole (confusable names).
Mixed affective episodes: bank keys sodium valproate (National Institute for Health and Care Excellence treats as mania); extra pool keys olanzapine.

sections.title: 3. The principles of rational prescribing of psychotropics

blocks.title: Principles of rational prescribing
rows: For depression and anxiety, National Institute for Health and Care Excellence recommends watchful waiting before pharmacological interventions
Lowest possible dose for the minimum duration possible; if expected improvement does not occur, the formulation and management plan must be revised
Many psychotropics have dose-dependent therapeutic and side effects; plasma monitoring can be useful in some circumstances (therapeutic window phenomenon, discussed later)
Metabolic side-effects arguably contribute to more days of life lost than any other adverse effects of psychotropics; classes have specific recommendations on frequency and extent of monitoring
A good follow-up schedule is essential to monitor effect; without it the purpose of pharmacological treatment fails
Most national guidelines explicitly recommend avoiding combinations of psychotropics, especially antipsychotics
Pros and cons of a treatment must be discussed in advance so the patient can make an informed decision

Guidelines such as National Institute for Health and Care Excellence recommend patients be supported to make the final choice of a specific psychotropic for an indication from options provided by the psychiatrist

blocks.mnemonic: Wise Students Treat Many Real Adults In Practice

blocks.text: Off-label use: not recommended for uncommon, non-specific indications, but not illegal per se in most countries; such practice often has flimsy or no evidence base. The prescriber must explain that the drug is being used outside its licensed indications and provide the available evidence of effectiveness.
Long-term prescriptions (chronic illness): follow relevant local and national guidelines; note which medications worked before and which did not, plus the adverse effects each produced.

blocks.caption: Boxed text: 'Chemistry & Storage' - defines hygrophilicity and deliquescence (sodium valproate given as the example).

blocks.title: Chemistry and storage
rows: Hygrophilicity (Reviewer correction (not in the source): hygroscopicity - NEEDS VERIFICATION)

Drugs exposed to moisture and light can gain moisture quickly, reducing availability of active excipients (Reviewer correction (not in the source): excipients are inactive by definition, so 'active ingredient' is probably meant - NEEDS VERIFICATION)
Some drugs are so sensitive to environmental moisture that they turn from crystalline states into pastes or liquids after brief contact with moist air; sodium **valproate** is the example given

blocks.note: **Q12**: all of **haloperidol** blood levels (higher peak after rapid tranquillisation in Asians than Caucasians), tricyclic hydroxylation (slower in Asians; Caucasians have lower tricyclic antidepressant plasma levels), alcohol metabolism (about ==40%== of Asians and ==60%== of South American Native Indians lack enough aldehyde dehydrogenase) and prolactin response to antipsychotics (greater in Asians) show ethnic differences. Not in the notes.

blocks.text: 'All of the listed options' is correct - don't stop at the first true statement. Ethnic differences are noted for **haloperidol** blood levels (higher peak plasma level in Asians after rapid tranquillisation), hydroxylation of tricyclics (slow hydroxylation more common in Asians), alcohol metabolism (aldehyde dehydrogenase lack) and prolactin response to antipsychotics (greater in Asians).

blocks.note: **Q54**: lack of aldehyde dehydrogenase creates natural alcohol deterrence (majority of north Asian origin are poor metabolisers via this enzyme). Not in the notes.

blocks.text: Natural alcohol deterrence = **LACK** of aldehyde dehydrogenase (it converts acetaldehyde to acetic acid); the explanation notes the majority of people of north Asian origin are poor metabolisers via aldehyde dehydrogenase. High aldehyde dehydrogenase, high alcohol dehydrogenase, low cholinesterase and high **CYP3A4** are the wrong options.

blocks.note: **Q23**: **lithium** (==95%== excreted unchanged in urine) has the same pharmacokinetics in Asians and White Europeans. Not in the notes.

blocks.text: **Lithium** is the psychotropic with the **SAME** pharmacokinetics in Asians and White Europeans: about ==95%== is excreted unchanged in the urine and excretion does not differ between the groups. **Alprazolam**, **haloperidol**, **diazepam** and **chlorpromazine** are the distractors.

blocks.subtopic: Predictors of poor response to lithium prophylaxis
blocks.note: Extra-pool question: predictors of poor response to **lithium** in bipolar prophylaxis include a high number of previous hospitalisations (the keyed answer), stress, high expressed emotion, a high number of life events, an episodic depression-mania interval pattern, continuous cycling, unemployment and neurotic personality. Not in the notes.

**Q11**: antipsychotic medication is first-line for first-episode psychosis (**olanzapine**, **amisulpride**, **risperidone** may be marginally better), choice made together with the patient considering adverse effects; the answer was low-dose **risperidone**. The notes discuss patient choice but not this scenario.

blocks.text: First-episode psychosis in a 15-year-old: antipsychotic medication is first-line, so low-dose **risperidone** - **NOT** parental training, family therapy, **fluoxetine** or **CBT** for anxiety. **Olanzapine**, **amisulpride** and **risperidone** may be marginally better than other options; the choice is made with the patient, considering the adverse effect profile.

blocks.note: **Q32**: when verbal de-escalation has failed, temporary physical or pharmacological restraint with frequent re-evaluation of medical status is the answer; only minimal restraint should be used. Not covered in the notes.

blocks.text: Agitated, combative elderly patient with dementia: use temporary physical or pharmacological restraint with regular re-evaluation - only a **MINIMAL** amount of restraint, re-evaluated frequently - not heavy sedation. Verbal de-escalation has already failed, discharge is wrong, and transfer to a psychiatric ward is not practical; involving a carer may help.

blocks.note: Extra-pool question: the most accurate statement is that 9-delta-tetrahydrocannabinol (**THC**) is the active substance (the most important of 60 psychoactive cannabinoids). Anandamide is a naturally occurring agonist at the cannabinoid receptor; cannabis is not usually associated with physical dependence; urine tests stay positive up to 4 weeks after regular use stops; there are no reports of fatal overdose. Not in the notes.
Extra-pool question: tolerance is the pharmacological adaptation because of which a larger dose of a drug becomes necessary over time to achieve the same effect (cocaine-user stem). Not in the notes.

bullets.text: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence: watchful waiting before drugs in depression and anxiety.
Start low, go slow: lowest dose for minimum duration; revise formulation/plan if no improvement.
Monitor: therapeutic (plasma levels where useful), metabolic (more days of life lost than other adverse effects), and response via follow-up.
Avoid polypharmacy, especially antipsychotic combinations.
Informed consent and patient choice (National Institute for Health and Care Excellence) of the specific drug.
Off-label use: not illegal per se but weakly evidence-based; explain the unlicensed use and evidence to the patient.
Long-term prescribing: follow guidelines and record what worked, what did not and adverse effects.
Hygrophilicity (Reviewer correction (not in the source), NEEDS VERIFICATION: hygroscopicity) = gaining moisture; deliquescence = turning to paste/liquid (sodium valproate).

Ethnic differences: all of haloperidol levels, tricyclic antidepressant hydroxylation, alcohol metabolism (ALDH lack) and prolactin response; lithium is the same in Asians and Whites (95% excreted unchanged).

blocks.title: Placebo terminology
rows: Any intervention deliberately used for non-specific psychological or psychophysiological treatment effect; may be pharmacologically active or inert (most commonly inert). Latin 'to please'; term coined by anaesthetist Beecher in 1955 (as the notes print). NEEDS VERIFICATION: Reviewer correction (not in the source): Latin 'I shall please'; the word was already in medical use before 1955 (the Q19 explanation cites Hooper's Medical Dictionary, 1811), and Beecher's 1955 paper 'The Powerful Placebo' began the modern study of the placebo effect
Any difference in outcome between a placebo-treated group and an untreated control group in an unbiased experiment (Ernst 2001)
Has some activity inherently, but not against the treated condition

A substance given for placebo effect that produces prominent side-effects; Latin 'I shall harm'. The nocebo effect is the negative consequences, adverse reactions and intolerance from giving a placebo; usually non-specific e.g. headache, nausea
Decrease in placebo effect with repeated or chronic administration of placebo drugs
Placebo effect may be disproportionately large for non-blinded therapies

blocks.text: Active placebo = has some activity inherently, but **NOT** against the treated condition (the option 'activity against the treated illness' is the trap). In trials, active placebos contain ingredients that cause some of the active intervention's adverse effects, so blinding is better. Nocebo (placebo producing prominent side-effects) and placebo sag (decrease with repeated use) are separate terms.

blocks.title: Placebo response rates
rows: ==25-50%== (depends on improvement criterion and other factors)

blocks.text: Placebos work best for pain, disorders of autonomic sensation, and disorders of factors under neurohumoral control (e.g. nausea, blood pressure, bronchial asthma). Depression, anxiety and phobias show good placebo response; more chronically ill patients show lower response. Placebos fail in hereditary degenerative disorders, toxic and metabolic syndromes and vascular events.
Placebo effects also occur with active drugs (e.g. analgesics, antidepressants); the net effect of a drug is the sum of its pharmacological effects and the placebo effect.

Physiological changes in opioids and gamma-aminobutyric acid have been proposed to explain some aspects of placebo action; the neuropeptide hypothesis holds for placebo analgesia but is not proven in other conditions such as depression.

Three factors are necessary for placebo action: the nature of the disease treated and the doctor-patient relationship, patients' expectations, and experience with treatment in the past. Gender, suggestibility scores and intelligence quotient do not affect placebo effect consistently.
Placebos are more effective for clinical than experimentally induced conditions. They work better for severe than mild pain, but mildly depressed patients respond better than severely depressed ones.

In depression and schizophrenia studies the difference between active-treatment and placebo groups grows gradually: little difference until about 2 weeks, full difference by 6 weeks, increasing progressively for several months.

There are no homogeneous placebo reactors: a placebo responder for one condition or doctor will not show the same response for another. Placebo 'run-in' periods in antidepressant trials, which eliminate placebo reactors before the trial, do not greatly lower placebo response or raise the drug-placebo difference, and reduce generalisability and the pragmatic nature of trials (excluded responders may be the most likely to benefit from active treatment, making estimates too conservative).

A placebo can be a procedure, not a medication (e.g. sham electroconvulsive therapy; sham surgery with only a skin incision). Placebo analgesia may be associated with decreased beta-adrenergic activity of the heart (decreased heart rate and low-frequency heart-rate variability).
Placebo response is higher in trials with more than 2 arms than in two-arm trials: in a three-armed trial participants know they have a 2/3 chance of active treatment versus 1/2 in a two-armed study.

People have individual traits that predispose them to be more or less responsive to certain stimuli; the interaction between the learned associations of the clinical situation and the person's particular biology produces a response.

blocks.title: Features of the intervention that strengthen placebo effect
rows: Capsules are perceived as stronger than tablets
Larger pills stronger than smaller pills
Multiple pills stronger than a single pill
Anxiety responded better to green tablets, depression to yellow tablets (Schapira et al. 1970)
Surgery is likely better than the others at eliciting placebo effects

blocks.title: Why does a placebo work? Proposed explanations
rows: Disorders that respond to placebo are inherently episodic (remission/relapse cycles), so improvement would have occurred anyway and placebo use is merely coincident
On repeated measurement the sample mean moves from extreme values toward the population mean, which may explain an apparent placebo response in control groups

Placebo as a behavioural intervention: classical conditioning (active medication = unconditioned stimulus; pills/capsules/syringes = conditioned stimuli; therapeutic benefit = unconditioned then conditioned response) plus visceral learning akin to operant conditioning (perceived improvement acts as an internal reward). Conditioning mediates unconscious physiological functions (e.g. hormonal secretion); expectation mediates conscious processes (pain, motor performance). Learned associations producing placebo effects can be acquired through conditioning, especially for immune or endocrine conditions. During placebo treatment the patient's belief in being treated may cause selective attention to symptom improvement and expectation
Endorphins mediate placebo analgesia; it is partially reversed by the opioid antagonist **naloxone**. The dopamine reward system is increasingly implicated in psychotropic placebo effects

blocks.text: '**NOT** mediated via' = nocebo response. Mediators named in the question are natural remission, classical conditioning, expectancy and operant conditioning; the explanation says expectancies, learning and classical conditioning underlie both placebo and nocebo effects.

blocks.title: Placebo response vs antidepressant response in depression
rows: Starts abruptly, occurs early in treatment
Less likely to persist (Quitkin et al. 1991)

blocks.text: Mayberg et al. (2002): patients whose depression remitted with fluoxetine or with placebo had nearly identical positron emission tomography brain scans, so the neurobiological correlates of placebo and drug response may not truly differ.

items.text: **Q19**: a placebo is a dummy preparation of inactive compound. The notes say Beecher coined the term in 1955; the explanation says 'placebo' entered Hooper's Medical Dictionary in 1811 and that Beecher began the modern study of the placebo effect (reconciled: Beecher began the modern study of the placebo effect but did not coin the word - NEEDS VERIFICATION).

**Q6**: opioids may have a role in placebo response (true). Wrong options: no placebo response in personality disorders, identifiable 'placebo reactors', similar response irrespective of treatment, and 'depression placebo response gradual but persistent' (notes: abrupt, early, less likely to persist).

**Q25**: true statement = prior therapeutic experiences can drive nocebo effects. Wrong: tablets better than capsules (capsules and larger pills are stronger), placebo not operating on active drugs (it does), severely depressed respond better, oral stronger than injections.

blocks.text: The anterior cingulate cortex is an important anatomical component of both the dopaminergic and the opioid system and has been activated during placebo analgesia.

blocks.note: **Q6** explanation: placebo effects are associated with release of endogenous opioids, endocannabinoids, dopamine, oxytocin and vasopressin (notes mention opioids, gamma-aminobutyric acid and dopamine only). **Q25** explanation: optimism, suggestibility and gender not closely associated with placebo responsiveness; nocebo more likely in those who are more anxious, with a history of medically unexplained symptoms or greater psychological distress.

bullets.text: Placebo: intervention used for non-specific effect (usually inert; Latin 'to please'; coined by Beecher 1955, per the notes). Reviewer correction (not in the source), NEEDS VERIFICATION: Latin 'I shall please'; Beecher 1955 ('The Powerful Placebo') began modern study of the effect, the word itself is older. Active placebo: some inherent activity, not against the treated condition.
Nocebo (Latin 'I shall harm'): negative non-specific effects e.g. headache, nausea; placebo sag = fall in effect with chronic use.
Placebo response: depression 25-60%, mania up to 25%, schizophrenia 25-50%, panic disorder up to 70%; lower in chronic illness.
No consistent placebo reactor; run-in periods do not much reduce placebo response and reduce generalisability.
Stronger placebo effect: capsules over tablets, larger pills, multiple pills, injections, surgery; more than two trial arms.
Explanations: natural remission, regression to the mean, conditioning (classical and operant/expectation), endogenous opioids (naloxone partially reverses placebo analgesia) and dopamine reward.
Placebo antidepressant response abrupt, early, less persistent vs gradual, later, persistent for drug; positron emission tomography scans nearly identical (Mayberg 2002).
Placebo works better for severe than mild pain, but mildly depressed patients respond better than severely depressed patients (tested in Question 25).
Placebos are more effective for clinical than for experimentally induced conditions.

Necessary factors: nature of the disease and the doctor-patient relationship, patient expectations, past experience with treatment. Gender, suggestibility and intelligence quotient do not affect placebo effect consistently.
A placebo can be a procedure, not a medication: sham electroconvulsive therapy, sham surgery with only a skin incision.

blocks.title: Steps before drug approval
rows: Molecule shown to have specific actions; extensive studies in at least two animal species; mutagenicity, carcinogenicity and organ system toxicity studied
Small group of volunteers; safety, tolerability and pharmacokinetics; usually open or uncontrolled
Hundreds of patients with the target disease compared with placebo to see if it works at all; controlled trials or small randomised controlled trials
Phase 3 (patients) - superiority or equivalence to standard
Extensive double-blind randomised controlled trials to determine how well it works and common side effects (comparative efficacy and tolerance profile)
After regulatory approval; less common side effects, sometimes leading to withdrawal, are picked up with large-scale prescribing

blocks.mnemonic: PSESP: Pre-clinical, Safety (phase 1), Efficacy (phase 2), Superiority (phase 3), Post-marketing (phase 4)

blocks.text: Regulatory agencies named: Food and Drug Administration (United States) and Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (United Kingdom).

rows: Thalidomide (analgesic, as printed in the notes; Reviewer correction (not in the source): thalidomide was a sedative/hypnotic used for morning sickness - NEEDS VERIFICATION)

blocks.text: **Q48**: mutagenicity, carcinogenicity and organ system toxicity are studied in the preclinical animal phase (not phase 1, 2, 3 or postmarketing); preclinical work also defines the therapeutic index to set starting doses in clinical trials.

**Q30**: thioridazine is the psychotropic well known to cause sudden death (QTc prolongation, torsades de pointes, sudden cardiac death; withdrawn from the global market in 2005; sertindole and **haloperidol** also cited). The notes' surveillance table lists thioridazine under QT interval prolongation and sertindole under sudden cardiac death - both stated.

Thioridazine is the high-**QT**-c answer: the explanation puts thioridazine, pimozide, sertindole and any intravenous antipsychotic at **HIGH** **QT**-c effect, while **chlorpromazine**, **quetiapine**, **ziprasidone** and tricyclics are only **MODERATE**. **Clozapine**, **olanzapine**, **haloperidol** and **chlorpromazine** are the other options offered.

Zimeldine = a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (the first selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor to reach the market: synthesised 1971, launched by Astra 1982, withdrawn the next year for adverse neurological effects / demyelination). The notes' surveillance table records hypersensitivity reactions and Guillain-Barre syndrome. Monoamine oxidase inhibitors, tricyclics, benzodiazepines and antipsychotics are the distractors.

blocks.note: **Q47**: 'standardised difference in effectiveness' is the difference in treatment effect between active and placebo groups after accounting for variation in the effect - the effect size (standardised mean difference or risk difference). Not in the notes.

bullets.text: Approval pathway regulated by Food and Drug Administration (United States) / Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (United Kingdom): preclinical, phase 1-3, then phase 4 post-marketing surveillance.
Preclinical: at least two animal species; mutagenicity, carcinogenicity, organ toxicity.
Phase 1 = safety/tolerability/pharmacokinetics in volunteers (open); phase 2 = effectiveness vs placebo in hundreds of patients.
Phase 3 = extensive double-blind randomised controlled trials for comparative efficacy and common side effects; phase 4 picks up rarer effects after approval.
Post-marketing hits: nefazodone/nomifensine hepatotoxicity; droperidol/thioridazine QT interval prolongation; sertindole sudden cardiac death.
Zimeldine: hypersensitivity and Guillain-Barre; remoxipride aplastic anaemia; mianserin blood dyscrasias; monoamine oxidase inhibitors cheese reaction; clozapine agranulocytosis.
QT-c: thioridazine, pimozide, sertindole and any IV antipsychotic = high effect; chlorpromazine, quetiapine, ziprasidone, tricyclic antidepressants = moderate.
Thalidomide: phocomelia, detected through post-marketing surveillance.

blocks.title: Compliance vs adherence vs concordance
rows: Extent to which a person's behaviour coincides with medical advice; implies sole patient responsibility; criticised as paternalistic
Includes patient choice: clinician and patient share responsibility; usually defined dichotomously in research, but rarely all-or-nothing
Therapeutic alliance between prescriber and patient as a negotiation process, with equal respect for both agendas

blocks.title: Adherence measurement tools
rows: e.g. Tablet Routines Questionnaire: daily routines for taking medication and proportion missed in the previous week and last month (Scott and Pope 2002)
Adherence (%) = (number of pills taken / number prescribed) x 100 (Azrin and Teichner 1998)
Devices on the tablet bottle record time and date of each opening
Frequency of dispensing as a proxy measure
Most objective; not available for all psychiatric drugs; expensive, invasive, limited value for partial adherence, overestimating adherence to long half-life drugs

blocks.text: Non-adherent patients with schizophrenia are 3.5 times more likely than adherent patients to relapse within 2 years.

blocks.caption: Three side-by-side boxes: 'Factors with no influence on adherence', 'Factors that reduce adherence' and 'Factors that increase adherence', each with a bulleted list.

blocks.title: Factors that reduce adherence
rows: Devaluation of medication effects by the physician
Oral formulations have poorer adherence than depots
Psychopathology of hostility, suspiciousness and disorganization

blocks.text: Patients with poor insight may still take medications - accepting the label is less important than enhancing awareness of drug effects.
Dose strength: the relationship with adherence is probably curvilinear - very low doses are associated with poor efficacy and very high doses with excessive side-effects.

blocks.title: Health belief model: four belief categories a patient weighs before deciding on prescribed medication
rows: Secondary benefits of medication and adherence

blocks.text: **Q16**: intentional non-adherence is linked with a low degree of self-efficacy (high self-efficacy and internal health locus of control consistently promote adherence). The explanation repeats the notes' points: lack of insight is the most common cause of poor adherence, and dose strength is probably curvilinearly related to adherence.

bullets.text: Compliance (patient-only responsibility, paternalistic) vs adherence (shared responsibility, patient choice) vs concordance (negotiated alliance, equal respect).

Measures: self-report (Tablet Routines Questionnaire), pill counts, electronic bottle caps, prescription monitoring, saliva/plasma/urine assays (most objective but costly, invasive, overestimate for long half-life drugs).
Pill-count adherence % = pills taken / pills prescribed x 100.
Non-adherence: antipsychotics 40-60%, mood stabilizers 18-56%, antidepressants 30-97% (median 63%); non-adherent schizophrenia 3.5x more likely to relapse in 2 years.

Lack of insight is the most common cause of reduced adherence; also fear of side effects, polypharmacy, high dose frequency, oral vs depot, maintenance treatment, hostility/suspiciousness/disorganization.
Increase adherence: family support, liquid or sublingual forms, enthusiastic clinician, good relationship, continued access.
No influence: age at onset, age at first hospitalization, sex, socioeconomic status, marital status, ethnicity.
Dose strength relation is curvilinear; health belief model: benefits, costs, susceptibility, secondary benefits.

facts.label: Most common cause of poor adherence

blocks.text: Adherence enhancement is possible if the patient's perceptions are altered. Most patient/family-directed psychoeducational programmes focus on imparting knowledge without attitudinal and behavioural change and are therefore largely ineffective at enhancing adherence.

blocks.title: Interventions to improve adherence
rows: Target patient's attitudes and beliefs about medication, to influence the personal construction of the meaning of medication and illness (Zygmunt et al. 2002)
Assume behaviour is learnt and can be modified; patients given instructions and strategies (reminders, self-monitoring tools, cues, reinforcements) (Zygmunt et al. 2002)
Enables the patient to express personal reasons for and against improving treatment adherence

Brief intervention based on motivational interviewing and cognitive approaches: ambivalence explored first, then consequences of stopping medication; analogies with chronic physical illness; pros and cons of medication considered

blocks.text: Mr Z (non-adherent schizophrenia, repeated relapses): cognitive motivational intervention is keyed - the explanation says psychoeducation alone and family therapy alone were ineffective, programmes focusing on attitudinal and behavioural aspects of taking medication do better, and there is no evidence base for supportive or insight-oriented psychotherapy.

bullets.text: Adherence improves if patient perceptions are altered.
Knowledge-only psychoeducation (patient/family) is largely ineffective as it ignores attitude and behaviour change.
Cognitive-based interventions target attitudes and beliefs about medication.
Behaviour modification: reminders, self-monitoring, cues and reinforcements.
Motivational interviewing: patient voices reasons for and against adherence.
Compliance therapy: brief MI + cognitive approach; explore ambivalence, then consequences of stopping; analogies with chronic physical illness.
Mr Z question: cognitive motivational intervention; psychoeducation alone and family therapy alone ineffective.
